title.en: Arnarkuak, the Woman Who Wanted to Be a Man
title.zh: 自居男子的女人阿納庫阿克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 92 'The Woman who wanted to be a Man', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Never ceasing to scold her son for his want of skill in hunting and other manly pursuits, Arnarkuak forces her daughter-in-law under threat of death to flee with her to the interior, where she disguises herself like a man and takes her daughter-in-law Ukquamak for a wife — but the son finds out their place of refuge, and kills his despicable mother.
summary.zh: 因兒子獵藝不精而無休止斥罵的阿納庫阿克，以死相逼，迫使兒媳烏夸馬克隨她遁入內陸；她扮作男子，把兒媳當作妻子——然而兒子尋得他們的藏身之處，殺死了那可憎的母親。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note; matricide recorded as told.

passages.text: A woman named Arnarkuak would not give up scolding her son on account of his want of skill in hunting and other manly pursuits. Once in his absence, when he had gone out kayaking, she forced her daughter-in-law, by threatening her with death, to flee with her to the interior of the country, where she disguised herself like a man, and had her daughter-in-law Ukquamak for a wife — but the son found out their place of refuge, and killed his despicable mother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 92 'The Woman who wanted to be a Man'; not verbatim.

title.en: An Angakok Flight: The Thong-Bound Wizard
title.zh: 巫師飛行：皮繩縛身的降靈

region.en: Inland houses of women and inlanders
region.zh: 內陸的女人之屋與內陸人營地

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 93 'An Angakok Flight', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Bound in a seal-skin thong from toe to head, the great angakok lifts the roof off his house and flies inland: a house inhabited only by women whose enchanted husband — a house-pillar — emits sparks of fire and lead at his approach; a second flight ends in the inlanders' ball-play, hurled nearly dead between them until his tornak rescues him; the third brings him to his sister lost many years before, now married to an inlander, who gives him a piece of reindeer-skin as a token that he had really been with her.
summary.zh: 以海豹皮繩自趾纏頭的大巫師，飛起時掀開屋頂；第一次飛行入內陸，遇一屋只有女人——那被施咒的丈夫（屋柱）見他靠近便迸出火星與鉛丸；第二次飛行落入內陸人手中，被他們當球拋擲，幾近喪命，賴靈助相救；第三次飛行尋得多年杳無音信的妹妹——她已嫁給內陸人，贈他一片馴鹿皮作為『確曾相會』的信物。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale per Rink's note; documents angakok flight binding ritual.

passages.text: A great angakok, being once called upon to perform a conjuration, took a thong of seal-skin, and having in one end cut a hole for his toe he twisted it round his body and made fast the other end to his head. When the lamps had been all extinguished he was lifted up, and soaring about the house he made the roof lift and give way to him. Having escaped through the opening he flew to the inland and came to a house inhabited only by women — but as soon as he tried to approach any of them the house-pillar (their enchanted husband) began to emit sparks of fire and lead towards him. The next time he flew to the inland he was seized hold of by the inlanders, who essayed to play at ball with him, hurling him backwards and forwards between them till he was nearly dead, when he called his tornak, who quickly rescued him. The third time he came to his sister, who had disappeared many years before, but whom he now found married to an inlander; she gave him a piece of reindeer-skin as a token to take home with him in order to convince people of his really having been with her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 93 'An Angakok Flight'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Means for Getting Children: The Two Little Dried Fishes

region.en: Far north and far south quest
region.zh: 遠北與遠南的尋求之旅

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 94 'The Means for getting Children', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Travelling a summer north and a summer south for a means to get children, a husband wins from an old woman two small dried fishes — male for a son, female for a daughter — but stricken with hunger on the long road home he reasons 'What is the use of keeping this spawner? A son is what we desire' and swallows the male fish. Growing bigger and bigger till he can hardly slip into his kayak, he is delivered by a skilful old woman's charm of what was encumbering his inside: a fine little daughter.
summary.zh: 為求子而一夏北上、一夏南下的丈夫，終於從老嫗處得來兩尾小魚乾——雄魚得子、雌魚得女；歸途飢餓難耐，他暗想『留著這尾雄魚何用？我們要的本是兒子』——一口吞下。此後他日益腹脹，連皮艇都難以容身；最後由一位通靈的老嫗施法，替他『分娩』出腹中之物——竟是個可愛的女兒。

sensitivity.note: Rink doubts whether the rest of the tale is of genuine Eskimo origin — noted as part of the source.

passages.text: A married couple had in vain been in hope of getting children; at length the man set out in search of some means to attain their desire. The first summer he travelled as far as he could get to the north, and the next as far as possible to the south, before he succeeded in finding an old woman who promised to help him. From the bottom of her bag she produced two small dried fishes, a male and a female, of which he was to give his wife the former to eat if he wanted a son, and the latter in case they preferred a daughter. He received the fishes and started on his way home; but having to travel very far and not always being able to get any victuals, once in a great strain for something to eat began to consider, 'What is the use of keeping this spawner? A son is what we desire' — on which he swallowed the one little fish. After a while he began to feel very ill at ease, at the same time growing bigger and bigger, till at length he could hardly manage to slip down in his kayak. A skilful old woman who lived at a place where he happened to land soon suspected what was the matter with him, and hit on a charm to deliver him of what was encumbering his inside, which soon proved to be a fine little daughter.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 94 'The Means for getting Children'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 康瓜克的兒子：追上獵隼的划手

region.en: Umanarsuak, high island of South Greenland
region.zh: 南格陵蘭烏馬納舒阿克高島

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 95 'Kanginguak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: The son of the southerner Kanginguak rows so expertly that he overtakes falcons in their flight and kills them with a blow of his paddle-oar; he rows out so far that Umanarsuak appears like a seal diving up and down among the waves — but in a match with a celebrated kayaker he is killed by his rival. His father afterwards goes to the place where he was buried, brings out his body again, and carries it along with him till he finds an angakok who restores it to life.
summary.zh: 南方人康瓜克之子划技超群：能追上飛掠的獵隼、以槳一擊斃之；出海之遠，使烏馬納舒阿克島看來如波間起伏的海豹——然而與名艇客比試時，他死於對手之手。父親隨後掘出他的遺體，一路攜行，直到尋得一位巫師將他救活。

passages.text: Kanginguak was a native of the south, who set forth on a journey and took up his abode near Umanarsuak (a high island of South Greenland). He had a son named Tunerak, who was such an expert rower that he used to overtake the falcons in their flight and killed them with a blow of his paddle-oar; he went out to sea so far as to make Umanarsuak appear like a seal diving up and down among the waves — he also tried matches with celebrated kayakers, but on one of these occasions he was killed by his rival. His father afterwards went to the place where he was buried, brought out his body again and carried it along with him till he found an angakok who restored it to life.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 95 'Kanginguak'; not verbatim.

title.en: Kigdlinararsuk: The Merganser Amulet in the Prow
title.zh: 基格德利納拉舒克：艇首的秋沙鴨符

region.en: The old hags' coast, northward quest
region.zh: 老嫗們的海岸，北行之路

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 96 'Kigdlinararsuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Out to avenge his sister's murder, Kigdlinararsuk seeks an old woman who can give an amulet for giving swiftness to a boat: the first confesses she has grown old to no purpose — 'I am only clever in...' (the words untranslatable, per Rink's note, being the humblest of crafts) — but has an elder sister more cunning farther north, who gives him a small bit of a dried merganser. Inserted into the prow so no marks or joints are visible, tried twice until the boat can run down a flying merganser, he starts at last to encounter his adversaries.
summary.zh: 為妹復仇的基格德利納拉舒克，尋求能賜舟以速的護身符：第一位老嫗自承『我白活了這把年紀，只會……』（其原話按注無從譯出，是一門最低微的手藝），但北邊有位更精明的姐姐——贈他一小片秋沙鴨乾。他把符片嵌入艇首，接口無痕；試了兩次，直到船能追上飛掠的秋沙鴨，方才啟程尋仇。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; Rink's note explains the omitted modest formula.

passages.text: Kigdlinararsuk, in order to avenge the murder of his sister, went out in search of an old woman who could assist him in getting an amulet for giving swiftness to a boat. The first one he came to replied, 'I have grown rather old to no purpose (viz., without having acquired wisdom), I am only clever in...' [words omitted] '...but farther north I have an elder sister more cunning than I; first try thy luck with her, and if thou dost not succeed I'll see what can be done.' He then went farther and came to another old hag, who gave him for an amulet a small bit of a dried Merganser; this he inserted in the prow of the boat with such care that no marks or joints were visible — twice he tried it before the boat appeared swift enough to run down a flying Merganser, and not till then did he start to encounter his adversaries.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 96 'Kigdlinararsuk'; not verbatim.

title.en: The Man of Karusuk and His Ingnersuak Companion
title.zh: 卡魯舒克與其精靈同伴

region.en: Karusuk in the firth of Godthaab and Kangek
region.zh: 努克峽灣的卡魯舒克與康格克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 97 'A Man living on Karusuk', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Every day a man of Karusuk repairs the twenty-four miles to Kangek to hunt auks, companioned by an ingnersuak who is also the tornak of an angakok farther up the firth at Tukak — in the short winter days it comes to Karasuk, waits till the man is ready to start, follows and takes care of him the whole day, and returns with him to Karusuk, whence it goes on to its home at Tukak. Two distinct kayaks seen at a distance become one close up: an ingnersuak, invisible excepting from a great distance.
summary.zh: 卡魯舒克的一名男子日日往返二十四哩外的康格克獵海鳩，同行者是一位精靈——同時也是上游圖卡克一位巫師的靈助。冬日晝短，精靈來到卡魯舒克，候他整裝出發，一路照看整日，隨他歸來後再自行返回圖卡克。遠處明明是兩條皮艇，近前只剩一條——那便是精靈：唯遠望可見。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale documenting ingnersuak companionship belief (compare tale 46).

passages.text: A man living on Karusuk (in the firth of Godthaab) every day used to repair to Kangek (about 24 miles distant) for the purpose of hunting auks. For his companion he had an ingnersuak, who at the same time was the tornak of an angakok living farther up the firth at Tukak. It is said that even nowadays many kayakers have an ingnersuak for their companion, and every now and then they become visible; sometimes a kayaker observing two distinct kayaks at a distance on coming nearer will only meet with one, who on being questioned is not aware of any other having been with him — in such cases people believe it to have been an ingnersuak, on account of their being invisible excepting from a great distance. The said ingnersuak in the short winter days came to Karasuk, waited until he saw the man ready to start for Kangek, and then followed and took care of him the whole day, and returned with him to Karusuk, from whence he went on to his home at Tukak.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 97 'A Man living on Karusuk'; not verbatim.

title.en: Atarsuatsiak: A Row of Murder-Marks Across the Forehead
title.zh: 阿塔舒阿茨夏克：額際一排殺人刺青

region.zh: 北格陵蘭烏珀納維克一帶

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 98 'Atarsuatsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Atarsuatsiak and his brothers were a set of fearful man-slayers living in the country about Upernivik, who had their heads tattooed with a separate mark for each murder they had committed — on Atarsuatsiak these marks formed a whole row along his forehead from one side to the other. At last the people of the neighbouring places resolved upon having him killed at a place to which he used to resort in order to visit his concubine.
summary.zh: 阿塔舒阿茨夏克與其兄弟是烏珀納維克一帶令人聞風喪膽的殺人者，每殺一人便在頭上刺一記號——阿塔舒阿茨夏克額際的刺青已連成一排，橫貫兩鬢。最後，鄰近各處的人合謀，在他常去會情婦的地方將他結果。

passages.text: Atarsuatsiak and his brothers were a set of fearful man-slayers, living in the country about Upernivik (Greenland), who had their heads tattooed with a separate mark for each murder they had committed; on Atarsuatsiak these marks formed a whole row along his forehead from one side to the other. At last the people of the neighbouring places resolved upon having him killed at a place to which he used to resort in order to visit his concubine.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 98 'Atarsuatsiak'; not verbatim.

title.en: Among the Last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak
title.zh: 康格盧克蘇瓦夏克的末代巫師

region.zh: 東格陵蘭康格盧克蘇瓦夏克

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary form, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 99 'Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Kapiarsuak and Avangnanersuak go out daily all winter to catch partridges and never bring any home, never seen to eat — a curious child accompanying them watches Kapiarsuak strike a flat rock with his staff and murmur certain words: an opening appears in the ground, out of which they angle up different kinds of food, giving the child a small fish to swallow after which it loses all remembrance — not until full-grown, many years after, does it suddenly recollect the event. Kuvatsiak, whose brother was seized by the ingnersuit, dreams like Akamalik, meets his dead brother at sea laboring under a black impediment on his kayak that alone hinders him from leaving the under-world people, and when the first missionary comes a dream induces him to get baptised.
summary.zh: 康加皮亞舒克與阿萬格納內舒亞克整個冬天日日外出『獵雷鳥』，卻從不帶回、也從不見進食；一個好奇的孩子隨行，目睹前者以杖擊平石、低聲念咒——地面裂開，二人自穴中垂釣取出各色食物，並給孩子吞下一尾小魚令其忘卻所見——多年後長大成人，他才驀然憶起此事。庫瓦茨夏克的兄弟被地下之民擄走；他得了一個類似阿卡馬利克的夢，老年時常在海上遇見亡弟——艇上那件黑物正是阻止他離開地下之民、重返人間的唯一障礙；首批傳教士到來時，一夢引他受洗。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tales documenting the last angakut generation; Christian syncretism noted in the source.

passages.text: Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak (Greenland) was a man named Kapiarsuk, and a woman called Avangnanersuak, who every day during the whole winter used to go out together to catch partridges, but never brought any home, and never were seen to eat anything at all. At last a child who was anxious as to their doings one day asked leave to accompany them, and soon observed that they never looked for any partridges at all — but having come a good way up the country Kapiarsuak commenced to strike a flat rock with his staff, and murmuring certain words an opening appeared in the ground, out of which they went on angling and hauling up different kinds of food, allowing the child to partake of the good fare. On going home they gave it a small fish to swallow, after which it lost all remembrance of what it had seen — not until he was full grown, many years after, did he suddenly recollect the event and narrate it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 99 'Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Another angakok of the same place, named Kuvatsiak, had two brothers, Usuinak and Igpak, of whom the former having gone out kayaking did not return and entirely disappeared — in the evening they saw the clothes of the missing brother moving about by themselves. Kuvatsiak forthwith began to conjure, by means of which he found out that he had been seized by the ingnersuit. Kuvatsiak had a dream somewhat like that of Akamalik; and when he began growing old he often met with his deceased brother out at sea — he observed some black thing lying on the top of his brother's kayak, who laboured in vain to rid himself of it, saying that that was the only impediment hindering him from leaving the under-world people and returning to the land of the living. When the first missionary came to the country Kuvatsiak had a dream that induced him to get baptised.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 99 'Among the last Angakut at Kangerdlugsuatsiak'; not verbatim.

title.zh: 阿通加克：拉布拉多故事

region.en: Labrador coasts, cannibal land, and the lame people
region.zh: 拉布拉多海岸、食人之地與跛足人之鄉

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from Labrador, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Pursuing a runaway wife, Atungak is feasted by cannibals on man's-and-wolves'-brains, then child's-and-walrus' flesh, eating dried reindeer with appetite while children's brains are sucked out around him; a sling-boy felled by a pyrites-stone leaves one booted leg under the bench — 'Ye have done very ill in taking that miserable Ajajusek, who ought to have served his younger brother for food.' Fleeing past the lame people ('they hopped about like so many ravens' — the wife's laugh is fatal), cutting all their sledge-lashings, past two fighting black bears and a pot boiling of itself, they meet at last a watcher at a seal's breathing-hole: their own son, left behind a child. They have travelled over the whole world without changing or getting old.
summary.zh: 追回逃妻的阿通加克被食人族以人腦拌狼腦、再以孩童肉拌海象肉設宴；夫婦只肯吃乾鹿肉，而席間孩童的腦髓正被吸食。持套索的少年被黃鐵礦石擊斃，凳下只剩一隻穿靴的腿——『你們抓走那可憐的阿亞尤塞克真是造孽，他本該留著給弟弟當飯吃的。』逃過跛足人之鄉（其妻笑他們『像一群跳躍的渡鴉』，險釀大禍）、割斷所有橇繩、穿過兩頭搏鬥的黑熊與自行沸騰的鍋，最後在呼吸孔旁守候的獵人竟是幼時遺落的兒子——他們環遊世界而容顏未改。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; Rink notes its curious similarities with the next (East Greenland) fragment from the most widely severed Eskimo countries. Cannibalism recorded as told.

passages.text: A man named Atungak had two wives; one of them having run away he pursued her in his sledge and soon overtook her. They then travelled together and came to cannibals, whose chief invited them to his house and set before them a dish of man's and wolves' brains mixed together; when they declined eating it another was served consisting of the flesh of a child and of a walrus — and this also being rejected, they brought in dried reindeer-flesh which they ate with hearty appetite. Meanwhile the people got hold of some children, and feigning to pet them they killed them and sucked out their brains. A young lad was also there who carried a sling wherewith to entangle strangers; when he approached Atungak with this design he was struck on the head with a piece of pyrites-stone and fell to the ground. Afterwards when his mother came from another house to look for him she only found one of his legs left lying under the bench with the boot still on it, by means of which she recognised it — she then exclaimed, 'Ye have done very ill in taking that miserable Ajajusek, who ought to have served his younger brother for food.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.

passages.text: Atungak and his wife travelling on came to a country the people of which were all lame; before they reached them the chief came to receive them and warned them against his people as being a very ill-natured set. Nevertheless when Atungak's wife saw their ball-playing she could not help laughing, and said that they hopped about like so many ravens — Atungak got very much afraid when he heard the bystanders repeating this. He at once cut asunder all the lashings of the sledges belonging to the lame people so that they could not pursue them; hastening from there they came to two black bears engaged in a fight, and no other way being left they were obliged to pass between them — after which they came to a pot boiling of itself which they could not avoid crossing over. Lastly they came to a man watching at the breathing-hole of a seal, and on speaking to him they recognised him as Atungak's son whom they had left behind a child — they had travelled over the whole world without changing or getting old. In the north caves and clefts in the rocks are still to be seen in which they are said to have rested.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 100 'Atungak, a Tale from Labrador'; not verbatim.

title.en: Malarsuak: A Story from East Greenland
title.zh: 馬拉爾舒亞克：東格陵蘭故事

texts.period: Inuit oral tradition; fragmentary tale from East Greenland, English edition 1875 (Rink)

source.work: Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (Blackwood, 1875), tale 101 'Malarsuak, a Story from East Greenland', IA talestraditionso01rink

summary.en: Sledding in search of his lost sister, Malarsuak finds her domesticated among cannibals; a hideous-looking youth comes into the house and is killed by a bear's tooth fastened into a stick — 'Is this not my miserable son here — I mean the one who ought to serve as food for his brothers?' Returning with wife and child, the cannibals rob them of the child; warned by the brother-in-law to cut all his place-fellows' sledge-lashings, Malarsuak forgets one — it comes speeding after him, he kills the driver, and makes his escape himself.
summary.zh: 乘橇尋妹的馬拉爾舒亞克在食人族中找到已為人婦的妹妹；一名奇醜的少年入屋，被他以縛棍的熊牙刺穿頭顱——『這不就是我不成器的兒子嗎？他本該留著給兄弟們當飯吃的。』攜妻帶子重訪時，孩子被食人族奪走；臨別依小舅子之勸割斷眾人橇繩，卻漏了一架——那橇疾追而來，他殺了趕橇人，自己逃出生天。

sensitivity.note: Fragmentary tale; parallel to tale 100 (Labrador) per Rink's note. Child-stealing recorded as told.

passages.text: A man named Malarsuak started in search of his lost sister. Travelling by sledge he came to houses inhabited by cannibals, with one of which he found his sister domesticated. A hideous-looking youth came into the house, whom Malarsuak killed by piercing his head with a bear's tooth fastened into a stick, whereupon the host threw the dead body under the bench — some time after a woman appeared, saying, 'Is this not my miserable son here — I mean the one who ought to serve as food for his brothers?' Malarsuak travelled homewards, but came back on a visit, bringing his wife and a little child with him; the cannibals robbed them of their child. When going to leave the brother-in-law tried to persuade him first to cut all the lashings of his place-fellows' sledges in order to prevent their pursuing the travellers — Malarsuak took his advice, but happened to forget one of the sledges, which came speeding after him; he killed the driver and made his escape himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Henry Rink, Tales and Traditions of the Eskimo (1875), tale 101 'Malarsuak, a Story from East Greenland'; not verbatim.
